body.content: Somewhere on Kalshi right now there is a market asking whether a Claude Monet painting sells for more than $110,747,000 before the season closes. Not 'a lot of money.' Not 'a record.' That exact figure, down to the last thousand — because that is the exact hammer price a single Monet already fetched, at Sotheby's New York, on a Tuesday evening in May 2019. On the July 16 Dollar Bets board the contract was priced at $0.24, meaning the market thinks there is roughly a 1-in-4 chance a 19th-century Impressionist beats his own personal best sometime in the next few months. A dollar on yes comes back about $4.17. Yellow tier. Toss-up money on a haystack.

The number itself has a real backstory. In 1890 and 1891, Monet painted roughly twenty-five canvases of haystacks in the fields near his home in Giverny, working the same stacks in different light and season until each one became less about hay and more about time itself. One of those paintings, 'Meules,' surfaced at Sotheby's Impressionist & Modern Art Evening Sale in May 2019. Six bidders fought over it for more than eight minutes. It sold for $110,747,000 — an auction record for Monet, and at the time, the auction record for any work of Impressionist art, period. The buyer who'd last sold it, back in 1986, made roughly 44 times their money. Only eight of the surviving Haystacks paintings are in private hands at all; the other seventeen are locked up in museums like the Met and the Art Institute of Chicago, which means the ones still allowed to change hands are exactly the kind of scarce asset that can produce a headline number like that.

Here's the part that makes the 24-cent price interesting: nothing close to $110 million has come up for sale. Sotheby's Paris ran an evening auction in April 2026 featuring two Monets that had been out of public view for over a century, pulled from the same private family collection. 'Vétheuil, Effet du Matin' sold for about $12.1 million — a French auction record for Monet, but not remotely a threat to the global one. The other, 'Les Îles de Port-Villez,' went for about $7.6 million. Add them together and you're still less than a fifth of the way to what 'Meules' pulled in six years ago. For this market to pay out, some Monet nobody has publicly listed yet would need to appear at a major fall sale and clear a bar that only one painting in history has ever cleared.
why the price isn't zero anyway

A 24% implied probability sounds generous for a bet against a nine-figure ceiling that's been breached exactly once. But art markets run on surprise inventory — a painting nobody knew was for sale, out of an estate or a divorce or a family finally willing to part with the thing that's hung over the fireplace since 1974. The 2026 season already produced two such surprises in Paris; either one could just as easily have been a Water Lilies canvas instead of a haystack field, and the ceiling for those has run past $70 million before. The market isn't really pricing 'will Monet get more famous.' It's pricing 'will an unlisted nine-figure painting surface in the next few months,' which is a much harder thing to know than it sounds, and exactly the kind of question a regulated exchange has no business turning into a tradeable contract — and yet.

The Hall of Filth exists for exactly this kind of market: the ones where the backstory is real, the number is real, and the only fictional part is pretending a 130-year-old haystack painting is a liquid, tradeable asset with a season. A dollar on Monet breaking his own record is a real, listed bet, priced this morning at 24 cents. The painting will not move. The record might. If you want the rest of today's markets that probably should not exist but absolutely do, the Dollar Bets board is rebuilt every morning.

faqs.q: What is the current Monet auction record?
faqs.a: $110,747,000 — set by 'Meules,' from Monet's Haystacks series, at Sotheby's New York in May 2019. It is the auction record for Monet and was, at the time, the auction record for any Impressionist work sold at auction.

faqs.q: Has the record come close to being broken in 2026?
faqs.a: No. The largest Monet sale of the 2026 season so far was 'Vétheuil, Effet du Matin,' which sold for roughly $12.1 million at Sotheby's Paris in April 2026 — a French auction record for the artist, but far short of the $110.7 million global record.

faqs.q: What does $1 return on the Kalshi Monet market?
faqs.a: On the July 16 Dollar Bets board the yes side traded near $0.24, so a winning $1 stake returned roughly $4.17 before fees. Volume was around $12,316 at the time; the live price will differ by the time you check it. Read the current market on Kalshi before acting.

faqs.q: Why are only some Monet paintings worth this much?
faqs.a: Scarcity. Only eight of the surviving canvases from the Haystacks series remain in private hands — the other seventeen are held by museums including the Met and the Art Institute of Chicago and are not for sale. The same scarcity logic applies to his other major series, like Water Lilies, which is why an unlisted painting surfacing from a private collection can move the record.
